docs.text: Ablation. Destroying a small area of heart tissue on purpose, for example by radiofrequency heating, to stop an arrhythmia.
Action potential. The rise and fall of the transmembrane voltage when a heart cell is excited.
Activation wavefront. The moving boundary between excited and resting tissue. Also called the front.
Active catheter tracking. Locating small receiver coils at a catheter's tip from MR signals so the scanner can follow it and steer the imaging plane; reported at up to 50 updates per second.
Adversarial example. An input changed slightly, often invisibly, so that a model gives a different output; for ECG models, a small added waveform.
AI agent. A program in which a model, usually a large language model, chooses step by step which tool to call, reads the result and continues until a goal is met or a step limit is reached.
Air kerma. The kinetic energy that X-rays release per unit mass of air, in gray (Gy); measured at a reference point it relates to the dose at the patient's skin.
Anisotropy. Direction dependence of a tissue property: heart muscle conducts faster, and has lower resistance, along its fibers than across them.
Arrhythmia. An abnormal heart rhythm.
Atrial fibrillation (AF). A fast, irregular rhythm of the upper chambers, without organized atrial activity.
Atrium (plural atria). One of the two upper chambers of the heart.
Attention. In a neural network, a weighted average of value vectors whose weights come from how well a query matches each key, normalized by a softmax. The building block of the transformer.
Audit log. An append-only record of every step an agent took: the tool, its arguments, the policy decision and the result, so a person can check the run afterwards.
Average precision (PR AUC). The area under the precision–recall curve, averaged over thresholds. Unlike the ROC AUC it falls when positives are rare.
Average symmetric surface distance (ASSD). The mean distance between two surfaces, measured from each to the other; a typical-error measure for segmentations.
Bayesian optimization. Choosing where to measure next by modelling an unknown function with a probabilistic surrogate, such as a Gaussian process, and maximizing an acquisition function.

Bipolar electrogram. The difference between the signals of two nearby electrodes. It acts like a spatial derivative: it keeps local detail and rejects distant activity, but depends on the bipole's orientation to the wavefront.
C-arm. A fluoroscopy system with the X-ray source and detector on opposite ends of a C-shaped arm that rotates around the patient.
Cardiac sarcoidosis. Inflammation of the heart by granulomas, which can cause conduction block and ventricular tachycardia; FDG PET can show active inflammation.
Cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI). The strip of right atrial tissue between the inferior vena cava and the tricuspid valve; the usual ablation target for typical atrial flutter.

Central-slice theorem. The 1-D Fourier transform of a projection equals the 2-D Fourier transform of the image along the line through the origin at the same angle; it is why projections at enough angles determine a CT slice.
Clique. A small group of electrodes, such as a triangle or a square, whose bipoles are combined to estimate the local electric field.
Cohen's kappa. Agreement between two raters or methods beyond what chance would give: (observed − expected agreement) / (1 − expected agreement).
Collocation point. A point where a governing equation is checked during fitting; it needs no measurement.
Computed tomography (CT). Imaging that measures X-ray attenuation along many lines through the body and reconstructs cross-sectional slices from those measurements.
Concordance index (C index). For a risk score, the share of comparable patient pairs in which the patient with the earlier event had the higher score; 0.5 is chance.
Conducting channel. A corridor of surviving tissue through scar that may carry a reentrant ventricular tachycardia; post-processing software can identify candidate channels on LGE.
Conduction velocity. The speed at which the activation wavefront travels through tissue, in m/s (1 m/s = 1 mm/ms).,
Conformal prediction. A method that turns a model's scores into a set of possible answers that contains the true one at a chosen rate, using a held-out calibration set.

Contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR). The difference between two tissues' mean signals divided by the noise standard deviation; it decides whether they can be told apart, and averaging n independent samples multiplies it by the square root of n.
Contrastive learning. Self-supervised learning that pulls the embeddings of matched pairs, such as two recordings of one patient, together and pushes unmatched pairs apart.

Core-conductor model. A model of a cell strand in which intracellular current flows along the strand and leaks out through the membrane; it gives membrane current as the second derivative of transmembrane voltage.
Cross-entropy. The loss most classifiers minimize: minus the log of the probability given to the true class.
Current dipole. A current source and an equal sink very close together; its strength is current times separation, and its potential falls as one over distance squared.
CUSUM. Cumulative sum: a running sum of deviations above a target, reset at zero, that raises an alarm when it crosses a threshold. Used to detect a lasting shift in a monitored quantity.
Data augmentation. Training on altered copies of the data (for example, flipped or noisier signals) so a model ignores the alteration.
Dataset shift. Any difference between the data a model was trained on and the data where it is used: in class mix (prior shift), in the recordings (covariate shift) or in what labels mean.

De-identification. Removing or coarsening information in health data so that it no longer identifies a person, for example by removing direct identifiers and grouping quasi-identifiers; the rules differ by country.
Decapolar catheter. A catheter with ten electrodes along its shaft.,
Dice coefficient. Overlap of a predicted and a true region: twice the shared area over the sum of the two areas, from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (identical).,
Double layer. A surface covered with current dipoles pointing normal to it; a uniform double layer's potential is proportional to the solid angle it subtends.
ECG gating. Using the electrocardiogram to keep only imaging data from a chosen part of the cardiac cycle, so that the moving heart appears still.
Edema (myocardial). Excess water in heart tissue after injury such as ablation; bright on T2-weighted MRI, it includes reversible injury and fades over time.
Eikonal equation. The equation v |grad T| = 1 linking an activation-time map T to the local conduction speed v.
Electrogram. The voltage an electrode records from currents crossing cell membranes nearby.
Embedding. A vector that represents an input, such as a beat or a sentence, so that similar inputs get nearby vectors.
Endocardium. The inner surface of the heart wall.
Ensemble. A set of models trained with different random choices; their spread is used as an uncertainty estimate.
Error budget. A list of the error sources in a chain of steps with their sizes; independent, unbiased errors add in quadrature, and biases add directly.
Expected improvement. An acquisition function: the average amount by which a new measurement is expected to beat the best value so far.
External validation. Testing a frozen model on data from another place or time that played no part in training or tuning.
Extracellular volume (ECV). The fraction of a tissue's volume outside cells. MRI estimates it from T1 before and after gadolinium and the hematocrit; scar and fibrosis raise it.
Far-field signal. Activity that an electrode picks up from tissue that is not directly under it.
FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose). A glucose analog labeled with fluorine-18; cells that use much glucose, including inflammatory cells, take it up and show on PET.
Feature attribution. A score for how much each input feature, such as each sample of an ECG, contributed to a model's output for one input.
Federated learning. Training one model across sites that keep their data; only model updates are shared.
Fibrosis. Replacement of heart muscle by connective tissue. In the atria it can be estimated on late-gadolinium MRI.
Fiducial localization error (FLE). The error in locating a landmark used for registration, in either the image or the map.
Fiducial registration error (FRE). The residual distance between registered landmarks after a fit; its expected value depends on the number of landmarks and FLE, not on their layout.
Filtered back-projection. CT reconstruction that filters each projection with a ramp in frequency and smears it back along its lines; without the filter the image is blurred.
Fluoroscopy. Continuous or pulsed X-ray imaging that shows a moving shadow image, used to guide catheters, sheaths and leads.
Focal loss. A cross-entropy that down-weights examples the model already gets right, so training attends to rare and hard ones.
Focal source. A small region from which activation spreads outward.
Fossa ovalis. The thin central part of the wall between the two atria, where a needle usually crosses from the right atrium to the left.
Foundation model. A large model pretrained on broad, mostly unlabeled data and then adapted to many downstream tasks.

Full width at half maximum (FWHM). The width of a blur between the two points where it falls to half its peak; for a Gaussian, about 2.355 standard deviations. Used to quote the spatial resolution of scanners.
Gadolinium contrast. An MRI contrast agent that shortens T1 in proportion to its concentration and stays outside cells, so it accumulates where there is more extracellular space.
Gaussian mixture model. A probability model that describes data as a weighted sum of normal distributions; fitted with the EM algorithm to find clusters without labels.
Gaussian process. A probability model over functions; given measurements, it gives a mean estimate and an uncertainty at every other point.
Geodesic distance. The length of the shortest path between two points that stays on a surface.
Graph convolution. A network layer that mixes each point's features with those of its neighbors on a graph, such as the vertices of a mapping mesh.

Grating lobe. A false, full-strength copy of an array's beam that appears when its elements are spaced more than half a wavelength apart for the steering used; echoes from it are drawn in the wrong direction.
Guardrail. A rule enforced outside the model that limits what an agent may do, such as a tool allowlist, a schema check or a human approval step.
Half-life. The time for a radioactive tracer's activity to halve; 109.73 minutes for fluorine-18.
Half-value layer (HVL). The thickness of a material that halves the intensity of an X-ray beam; for a narrow beam of one energy it is ln 2 divided by the attenuation coefficient.
Hallucination. Output of a language model that reads as fluent and confident but is false or unsupported, such as an invented number or reference.
Hausdorff distance. The largest distance from any point of one surface to the other surface, in either direction; one stray island sets it.
Hematocrit. The fraction of blood volume made up of red cells; gadolinium in blood is confined to the rest, the plasma.
Hounsfield unit (HU). The CT number scale, 1000 (μ − μ_water)/(μ_water − μ_air): water is 0 and air −1000. Values depend on the X-ray beam's energy.
Human approval step. A point in an agent's run where a person must accept or decline an action, such as any write, before it is carried out.

Image intensity ratio (IIR). An LGE wall intensity divided by the mean blood-pool intensity, used to compare scans that have no absolute intensity scale; thresholds on it define atrial fibrosis or scar.
Implantable loop recorder (ILR). A small device placed under the skin that records the ECG for years and sends alerts when its detector fires.
Integrated gradients. A feature-attribution method that averages the model's gradient along a straight path from a baseline input to the actual input; the attributions add up to the change in output.
Interventional MRI. Performing a procedure, such as catheter ablation, inside an MRI scanner with real-time images instead of fluoroscopy.
Intracardiac echocardiography (ICE). Ultrasound imaging from a catheter inside the heart, used during procedures to see anatomy and build shells.
Intrinsic deflection. The steepest downstroke of a unipolar electrogram, used to mark local activation.
Inversion recovery. An MRI preparation that flips the longitudinal magnetization with a 180° pulse and reads the image while it recovers; a tissue has no signal at T1 ln 2.
Iodinated contrast. An iodine-containing agent injected into the blood; iodine attenuates X-rays strongly, so the blood pool stands out from the heart wall on CT.
Isocenter. The point a C-arm rotates about; structures there are imaged at a fixed magnification.
Isthmus (VT). A narrow channel of conducting tissue, bounded by scar or anatomical barriers, that a reentrant ventricular tachycardia passes through.
Jaccard index. Overlap of two regions as intersection over union; Dice = 2J/(1 + J).
k-anonymity. A property of a released table: every record shares its quasi-identifier values with at least k − 1 others, so a match by those values points to at least k records.
Kerma-area product (KAP). Air kerma times the area of the X-ray beam, in Gy·cm²; the same at any distance along the beam, so it describes the total radiation delivered. Also called dose-area product.
Large language model (LLM). A transformer trained on very large amounts of text to predict the next token; it can follow instructions and answer questions in text.
Larmor frequency. The frequency at which nuclear magnetization precesses in a magnetic field: 42.58 MHz per tesla for protons, about 64 MHz at 1.5 T.
Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). MRI taken some minutes after a gadolinium contrast injection, when scar and fibrosis appear bright.
Lead field. An electrode's sensitivity to sources everywhere: by reciprocity, the gradient of the potential it would create by injecting unit current.
Leave-one-patient-out. A test scheme that trains on all patients but one and tests on that one, in turn, so no patient is in both sets.
Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO). A catheter procedure that closes the left atrial appendage with an implanted device.
Lesion gap. A segment of an intended ablation line where the tissue was not destroyed, through which conduction can recover.
Lesion metabolic activity. A PET measure of a lesion: its partial-volume-corrected mean uptake times its volume.
Levenberg–Marquardt method. An iterative method for nonlinear least squares that blends Gauss–Newton steps with damped gradient steps.

Likelihood ratio. How much a test result changes the odds of disease: for a positive result, sensitivity divided by one minus specificity; for a negative result, one minus sensitivity divided by specificity. Post-test odds are pre-test odds times the likelihood ratio.
Linear probe. A linear classifier trained on the frozen features of a pretrained model, used to measure how much those features already encode.
Local activation time. The moment the activation wavefront reaches a given site.
Low-voltage area. A region whose bipolar voltage falls below a chosen cut-off. It is often read as scar, but the voltage also depends on the catheter and the wavefront.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Imaging of hydrogen nuclei in a strong magnetic field, with contrast from how their magnetization relaxes and position encoded by field gradients.
Magnetohydrodynamic voltage. A voltage induced when conducting blood flows across a strong magnetic field; it distorts the ECG and electrograms inside an MRI scanner.
Magnification (projection). How much larger a structure appears on the detector than its true size: source-to-detector over source-to-object distance.
Membrane current. Current crossing the cell membrane, positive outward; ahead of a wavefront it flows out (a source) and behind it flows in (a sink).

Method of images. Solving a problem with a flat boundary by adding mirror sources that make the boundary conditions hold; for two conductors the mirror source has strength (sigma1 - sigma2)/(sigma1 + sigma2) times the original.
Model card. A short document released with a trained model that states its intended use, out-of-scope uses, training and evaluation data, metrics overall and by group, and limitations.
Myocardial infarction. Death of an area of heart muscle caused by loss of its blood supply.
Negative predictive value (NPV). The share of negative results that are truly negative; like the positive predictive value, it depends on prevalence.
Net benefit. In decision-curve analysis, true positives minus false positives weighted by the odds of the threshold probability, per patient. It compares a model with acting on everyone or no one.
Normalized surface Dice (NSD). The share of two surfaces lying within a chosen tolerance of each other.
Omnipolar electrogram. A signal built from a clique by estimating the local electric field and reading it along the direction of propagation, which removes most orientation dependence.
Otsu's threshold. The intensity cut that splits a histogram into two classes with the largest between-class variance; used as a data-driven threshold for scar.
Out-of-distribution (OOD) input. An input unlike the data a model was trained on, such as a recording from a new device or with heavy noise, for which its outputs are not reliable.
Outflow tract. The part of a ventricle leading to its great artery (pulmonary artery on the right, aorta on the left); a common origin of idiopathic premature ventricular beats.
Pace mapping. Pacing from a catheter at candidate sites and comparing the paced 12-lead ECG with the ECG of the arrhythmia, to find where the arrhythmia starts.
Pacing. Stimulating the heart electrically from an electrode at a chosen site.

Partial-volume effect. A voxel, or a region blurred by the scanner, that holds more than one tissue reads a mixture of their values, so thin or small structures lose contrast and change apparent size.
Passive catheter visualization. Seeing a catheter on real-time MR images through the signal void or artifact its materials cause; it shows one plane at a time.
Phase-sensitive inversion recovery (PSIR). An LGE reconstruction that keeps the sign of the recovering magnetization, so it is much less sensitive to the chosen inversion time than a magnitude image.
Phased array. A row of transducer elements whose firing delays steer and focus the beam electronically, without moving the probe.
Photoplethysmography (PPG). Measuring blood-volume changes in tissue with light; the basis of pulse sensing in watches and trackers.
Physics-informed neural network (PINN). A neural network trained on a loss that adds the residual of a governing equation to the data misfit.
Point-spread function (PSF). The image an imaging system makes of a single point: the blur it applies to everything it shows.
Poisson's equation. The equation the potential obeys in a volume conductor, div(sigma grad phi) = -I_v: Ohm's law plus current conservation.
Positive predictive value (PPV). The share of positive results (alerts, flags) that are truly positive; it depends on prevalence.,
Positron emission tomography (PET). Imaging of a tracer that emits positrons; each annihilation sends two photons in opposite directions, detected together to define a line through the source.
Pre-test probability. The probability of a condition before a test result is known, for example its prevalence in the group tested.

Predetermined change control plan (PCCP). A plan, authorized with an AI-enabled device's marketing submission, that describes planned changes to the device and how each will be validated, so those changes need no new submission.
Premature beat. A beat that comes earlier than expected, usually followed by a longer interval; a common cause of false AF alerts.
Premature ventricular contraction (PVC). An extra beat that starts in a ventricle earlier than the next normal beat.
Prompt injection. Text inside a document or tool output that tries to make a language model follow new instructions, such as a hidden request to delete files.
Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI). Ablation that encircles the pulmonary veins so that their electrical activity cannot reach the left atrium.,
Pulmonary vein reconnection. Recovery of conduction between a pulmonary vein and the left atrium after isolation, usually through a gap in the lesion line.

Quantization (integer). Storing a model's weights or activations, or a signal's samples, as integers with a scale and zero point instead of floating-point numbers; it saves memory and computation at the cost of rounding error.
Quantum noise. Image noise caused by the random arrival of photons; with Poisson counts its standard deviation is the square root of the mean, so noise falls only as the square root of dose.
Quasi-identifier. A field that does not name a person on its own but can identify them in combination with others, such as age, sex, region or a procedure date.
Quasi-static approximation. Treating bioelectric fields as if they followed their sources instantly, neglecting capacitive, inductive and propagation effects in the volume conductor.
Radial basis function. A function of the distance to a centre, such as a Gaussian; sums of them represent smooth maps.
Radon transform. The set of line integrals of an image over all lines in the plane, indexed by angle and offset; a CT scanner measures it.
Randomized controlled trial (RCT). A study that assigns participants at random to an intervention or a comparison, so that differences in outcome can be attributed to the intervention.
Receptive field. The stretch of input that one output of a network depends on.
Reciprocity. Helmholtz's result that the potential a source produces at an electrode equals the source dotted with the field the electrode would create by injecting unit current.
Recovery coefficient. The fraction of a structure's true uptake (or contrast) that a blurred image measures; well below 1 for structures about as thin as the resolution.

Reference level (radiation dose). A benchmark for the typical dose of a procedure type, set from surveys (for example the third quartile of recorded doses); used to compare and optimize practice, not as a limit for one patient.
Reference standard. The best available method for deciding whether a condition is present, against which a test or model is judged; its own errors limit any measured accuracy.
Remote monitoring. Sending data from an implanted or wearable device to a clinic, where alerts are reviewed.
Repetition time (TR). The time between successive excitations in an MRI sequence; a real-time frame takes about the number of lines times TR.
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Answering with a language model after giving it passages retrieved from a chosen document collection, so that the answer can rest on, and cite, those passages.
RR interval. The time between two successive R peaks of the ECG, one ventricular beat to the next.
Scar. Fibrous tissue that has replaced heart muscle. It conducts poorly or not at all.
Segmentation. Labelling which voxels of an image belong to a structure, such as the left atrium.
Self-supervised learning. Learning representations from unlabeled data with a training task built from the data themselves, such as matching two views of one recording.
Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). Tomographic imaging of a tracer that emits single gamma photons, whose direction is set by a collimator.
Sinogram. The Radon transform drawn as an image: one row of line integrals per projection angle. A point traces a sine curve in it.
Sinus rhythm. The normal heartbeat, started by the heart's own pacemaker.
Softmax. The function that turns a vector of scores into probabilities that are positive and sum to one.
Solid angle. The area a surface covers on a unit sphere centered on the observer, in steradians; a full sphere is 4 pi.
Source and sink. Places where current leaves cells into the extracellular space (source) or enters them from it (sink); every source has a matching sink.
Spatial frequency. How quickly a pattern varies in space, in rad/mm. Fine detail has high spatial frequency.
Spatial resolution. How close two structures can be and still appear separate in an image; often quoted as the FWHM of the point-spread function.
Speed-of-sound assumption. Ultrasound systems convert echo time to depth with one assumed speed of sound, commonly 1540 m/s; tissue that is faster or slower is drawn shorter or longer.
Standardized uptake value (SUV). PET activity concentration divided by the injected activity per unit body weight, after decay correction; 1 means uniform distribution.
Surrogate model. A fast approximation of a slow model, fitted to runs of it and valid only in the range it was trained on.
T1 (longitudinal relaxation time). The time constant with which magnetization along the field recovers after it is disturbed; gadolinium shortens it.
Target registration error (TRE). The error after registration at a point not used for the fit, such as an ablation target; it grows with distance from the landmarks.
Temporal resolution. How short a time span one image represents. In cardiac CT it is about half the gantry rotation time with one X-ray source and a quarter with two.
Test-retest variability. How much a measurement changes when repeated on the same subject with nothing changed; it sets the smallest change that can be trusted.

Tetralogy of Fallot. A congenital heart defect affecting the right ventricular outflow and the ventricular septum. After surgical repair, ventricular tachycardia can use isthmuses bounded by patches and scars.
TF-IDF. Term frequency times inverse document frequency: a word weight that grows with how often the word appears in a document and with how rare it is across the collection.
Token. A unit of text, often a word or part of a word, that a language model reads and writes.
Tool schema. The declared arguments of an agent's tool, with their types, units and allowed ranges, checked before the tool runs.
Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). Ultrasound imaging of the heart from a probe in the esophagus, behind the left atrium.
Transformer. A neural-network architecture built from attention layers; the basis of most large language models and of many ECG foundation models.
Transmembrane voltage. The voltage across a cell membrane, inside minus outside.
Transseptal puncture. Crossing from the right atrium to the left atrium through the interatrial septum, usually at the fossa ovalis, with a needle and sheath.
Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE). Ultrasound imaging of the heart from a probe on the chest wall.
Unipolar electrogram. The signal of one electrode measured against a distant reference electrode. It sees local and far-field activity.
Ventricle. One of the two lower chambers of the heart.
Ventricular tachycardia. A fast rhythm that starts in the ventricles.,
Volume conductor. The conducting medium (tissue and blood) through which currents spread from their sources to the electrodes.

WFDB format. The Waveform Database format used by PhysioNet: integer samples in a signal file and a text header that gives the sampling rate, gain, baseline and units needed to convert them to physical values.
